extracted.intended_audience: readers of comedy criticism / stand-up fans and people who follow stand-up specials
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and judgement used by a critic to rate and discuss filmed stand-up comedy specials (what makes a special funny, artful, watchable, or disposable). Useful for critics, fans, and creators assessing specials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funniness / Consistency of laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: How consistently the special makes the reviewer laugh across the hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Kevin Hart made me laugh more consistently' — a special that elicits frequent, reliable laughs scores higher. Anti-pattern: specials that have only intermittent or one-off good jokes and otherwise lag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art / Craft
rubrics_metrics.description: The quality of the comedian's craft — structure, voice, originality and overall artistic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Sarah’s is better art. Of course... Sarah’s craft is undeniable.' Tradeoffs: a special can be funnier but less artful; critics may prefer craft over pure laugh counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality vs Predictability ('brave' vs obvious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the comedian brings fresh perspectives or merely rebrands predictable views as 'brave.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example/anti-pattern: Bill Maher 'I’m the only one brave enough to say this' but is 'just saying what half the country is already thinking.' Valuable comedy is genuinely surprising or insightful; predictable provocations score poorly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling coherence / narrative work
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the special tells a coherent story or carries a narrative arc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Andrew Schulz: 'the storytelling felt off and I couldn’t get into the whole journey.' If the narrative feels disjointed, the special loses engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format/gimmick effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether structural devices or gimmicks add to or distract from the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rosebud Baker's pregnant/not-pregnant editing: 'the format distracted more than it added.' Use of gimmicks should enhance material; if distracting, they detract from the special.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality / originality of material (avoid 'hack')
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the jokes feel fresh and well-crafted versus hacky, derivative, or low-effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Chris DiStefano: 'Hack.' Anti-pattern: 'Hularious brand... where comedians go when they are on their way down' — implies formulaic, unoriginal content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer energy / delivery style
rubrics_metrics.description: The energy and delivery the comedian brings onstage and whether it suits the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Liza Treyger 'Like the energy, didn’t love the material.' Delivery can elevate middling material; misaligned energy can harm it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crowd awareness and responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the performer pays attention to and works with the audience reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Iliza Shlesinger: 'recites her act with no regard whatsoever to how the crowd reacts. It’s like a robot performing comedy.' Anti-pattern: ignoring crowd cues makes a performance feel mechanical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Believability / authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the material feels truthful or believable to the critic — emotional honesty/authenticity in the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Joe List: 'I didn’t believe a word was true, and I need believability from my comedians.' Exaggeration is acceptable, but some 'real' anchor is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing / engagement (start-to-finish)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the special is paced to sustain interest (not starting too slow or dragging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: David Spade: 'Started too slow and I lost interest.' A slow start or dragging bits reduce the special's effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency / presence of 'off nights'
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an otherwise strong comedian can still produce weak specials — evidence of inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bill Burr: 'Even Burr has off nights.' Recognize that big names can produce underwhelming hours; consistency matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal taste / filthiness tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which a critic's taste (e.g., tolerance for 'filth') affects judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Steph Tolev: 'Filth isn’t my thing.' This is an explicitly subjective axis — some specials will be good to some audiences and off-putting to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform alignment: populist vs prestige programming
rubrics_metrics.description: How the special fits the platform’s tendencies (streamers often target populist vs prestige comedy) and whether that affects quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Netflix is still king, but they’re clearly pivoting toward populist comedy... HBO/Max continues to make smarter picks.' Consider whether the platform’s strategy colors the work and its ambition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution strategy / ownership and reach
rubrics_metrics.description: The business/distribution choice (YouTube vs streamers) and how that affects control, audience, and success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Comedians going to YouTube... he owns it, he controls it, and with 1.3+ million YouTube subscribers, he’s got the audience.' Independent release can be strategically better for some comedians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional signals (trailers / early marketing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether promotional materials (trailers) and early marketing accurately signal quality and tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kumail Nanjiani: 'the trailer wasn’t great' — trailers can set expectations and influence pre-release buzz; poor trailers may cloud reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversy / provocation and expected reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: How provocative material will be received and whether the comedian handles controversy in a way that serves the comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ricky Gervais: 'Expect the usual debate about Ricky saying things he "shouldn’t" and Ricky doubling down.' Provocative takes can be funny but invite predictable debates that affect reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watchability / immediate engagement for casual viewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a special appeals to general audiences or only to 'snob' critics; immediate watchability and mass appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I sometimes say of specials, "Civilians will like it." I’m a comedy snob and I never felt this one.' Some specials are crowd-pleasing even if critics find them lightweight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release timing and media coverage impact
rubrics_metrics.description: How release dates (e.g., holiday timing) affect media attention and list inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Tom Segura: Christmas Eve release. Won’t get the media coverage it might at a different time of year.' Timing can change visibility and awards consideration.
